title: What to Do If You Find a Hidden Camera in Your Rental
excerpt: Found a camera in your Airbnb or rental? Do not unplug it yet. Follow these steps to document it, protect yourself, report it, and get rehoused safely.
author: HiddenCameras Editorial Team
authorBio: The HiddenCameras.tv editorial team researches and writes about security cameras, surveillance technology, and home safety.
body:
Finding a lens staring at you from a smoke detector or an alarm clock turns a holiday into a cold knot in your stomach. The most important thing is that what you do in the next hour determines whether the situation gets resolved or gets muddy. Do not rip the device off the wall. Do not confront anyone in person. Document first, protect yourself second, and report through channels that leave a record.

This guide walks through exactly that sequence: preserving evidence without touching the device more than you must, covering the immediate privacy problem, contacting the host and the platform in the right order, involving local police when appropriate, and handling the aftermath. Laws vary by state and country, so treat this as practical guidance and check the rules in your own jurisdiction.

Pause and take stock before you touch anything

Your instinct will be to unplug it or cover it instantly. Resist that for just long enough to preserve the scene. An untouched device with its indicator lights, cables, and mounting tells a clearer story than one that has been yanked out. Investigators and platform safety teams both prefer to see the camera as you found it.

If the camera is in a bedroom, bathroom, or changing area, the violation is at its most serious in most jurisdictions. Note the room, what the camera points at, and whether it appears powered on — a glowing LED or a cable running to an outlet. Do not open it or try to view any memory card on your own devices.

Photograph everything while it is still in place

Use your phone and capture the scene thoroughly. Take wide shots showing the camera's position in the room, then close-ups of the lens, cables, mounts, and indicator lights. Stand beside the camera and photograph what it faces — the bed or seating area — so its field of view is documented.

Then capture context: the listing photos and house rules showing whether any camera was disclosed, your booking confirmation, and any messages with the host. Screenshot the listing's disclosure section if the platform has one. Back everything up to cloud storage immediately.

Cover it and reclaim the room for tonight

Once documentation is done, block the lens with a towel, tape, or a jacket. If it has an obvious plug, you may unplug it after photographing the connected state — photograph first, unplug second. Do not dismantle it or take it with you when you leave.

Decide whether you can sleep there tonight. If the camera was the only one and it is now covered or unplugged, staying until the platform relocates you may be reasonable. If there could be others, if the host's behaviour alarms you, or if you simply do not feel safe, leave — a nearby hotel or a public late-night venue while you call support is better than a night spent wondering.

Sweep the rest of the space quickly

Before settling, do a fast check of the other sensitive spots: smoke detectors with an odd lens glint, alarm clocks or chargers facing beds, and any device with an unexplained cable. Turn the lights off to spot unfamiliar standby LEDs. Save the check for daylight.

What to say to your host, word for word

Keep every message in writing on the platform's messaging system. Stay factual and do not accuse — you need a clear written record, not a heated exchange. Something like this works:

Hello, during our stay at [property address, check-in date] we found what appears to be a recording device in [room, e.g. the bedroom smoke detector]. I have photographed it in place. It was not disclosed in the listing. Please explain what this device is. I am also reporting this to [platform] support.

Do not agree to meet the host alone, and do not let anyone into the property to collect the device before you have reported it. If the host becomes hostile, stop communicating and go straight to the platform and local police.

Report in the right order: platform first, then police

Contact the booking platform's safety team immediately — most major platforms have an emergency line for exactly this. Share your photos, the listing link, and the host messages. Ask for relocation help and a refund, and note the case number.

Then contact local police on their non-emergency line unless you feel in immediate danger, in which case use the emergency number. Bring your photos, booking paperwork, and the host correspondence. Ask for a report number even if no arrest follows — platforms treat a police report number as the marker of a serious complaint.

What officers and support teams will ask you

Expect questions about when you arrived, when you noticed the device, and whether you moved it. Stick to what you observed rather than speculating about who installed it.

After the stay: refund, review, and your next booking

Once you are safe, follow up in writing on the refund, attaching the police report number. Keep receipts for alternative accommodation — platforms sometimes reimburse these, but only with paperwork.

When writing a review, state only verified facts: the room, the device, the lack of disclosure, and the case numbers. Avoid speculation about motives or claims about footage you have not seen. For future stays, filter for listings with explicit camera disclosures and do a two-minute lens check of sleeping areas on arrival.
